strengths: Conceptual novelty and clear intuition: Formulating tokenizer representation learning through downstream-aligned latent denoising (via interpolative noise and patch masking) is conceptually elegant and provides a fresh perspective beyond standard pixel-reconstruction VAEs.

Comprehensive and cross-paradigm evaluation: The paper thoroughly validates the approach across six diverse generative models spanning both autoregressive (MAR, RandomAR, RasterAR) and non-autoregressive/diffusion (DiT, SiT, LightningDiT) frameworks.

Insightful discovery on tokenizer transferability: The work reveals that popular semantics-distilled tokenizers fail drastically when transferred to autoregressive models, whereas l-DeTok achieves consistent gains across both paradigms without relying on heavy external pretrained models (e.g., DINOv2 or CLIP).

Strong empirical gains: On ImageNet 256x256, l-DeTok substantially pushes the frontier of continuous autoregressive models, improving MAR-B from 2.31 to 1.55 FID and MAR-L from 1.78 to 1.35 FID, matching or outperforming prior much larger models.

Detailed ablations: Extensive studies effectively isolate and justify critical design choices, including interpolative vs. additive latent noise, noise variance scale, random vs. constant masking ratio, and joint corruption.
weaknesses: Scope limited to ImageNet-256 and continuous tokenizers: The empirical validation is focused strictly on ImageNet class-conditional generation with continuous latent embeddings; exploration on discrete/VQ tokenizers or open-domain text-to-image datasets is left as future work.

Train-inference mismatch and decoder fine-tuning overhead: Because the tokenizer decoder is trained on heavily corrupted latents, an additional 100-epoch clean-latent decoder fine-tuning stage is required to fully resolve the distribution gap, introducing extra training cost.

Gap with semantics distillation on pure diffusion models: While l-DeTok decisively beats all standard non-distilled tokenizers across all models and excels on AR models, semantics-distilled tokenizers (e.g., VA-VAE) still hold an edge in FID on diffusion architectures like LightningDiT.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and well-motivated concept: aligning the training objective of visual tokenizers with the downstream generative task (denoising corrupted representations) is intuitive and conceptually neat.
Comprehensive experimental validation across both autoregressive (MAR, RandomAR, RasterAR) and non-autoregressive/diffusion-based models (DiT, SiT, LightningDiT).

Reveals a significant and previously underexplored finding: semantics-distilled continuous tokenizers (e.g., VA-VAE, MAETok) degrade heavily when applied to autoregressive generation (FID degrading to 15.88–38.13), whereas l-DeTok generalizes robustly across both paradigms without requiring external large-scale pretrained teachers.

Remarkable performance gains: MAR-B equipped with l-DeTok improves FID from 2.31 to 1.55, matching the much larger MAR-H (943M vs. 208M parameters), and MAR-L reaches an impressive 1.35 FID on ImageNet 256x256.
Thorough ablations: clearly dissects the role of interpolative vs. additive noise, noise scale gamma, masking strategies (random vs. fixed ratios), and encoder/decoder dynamics.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined strictly to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; validation on broader text-to-image tasks or higher resolutions (e.g., 512x512) would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

Training/inference discrepancy: the tokenizer decoder is trained primarily on heavily corrupted latents while operating on uncorrupted latents at inference time. Resolving this requires an additional 100-epoch decoder fine-tuning stage, increasing computational overhead.
Scope is limited to continuous latent spaces; whether similar latent denoising strategies benefit discrete vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizers remains unaddressed.

strengths: Clear and intuitive core concept: Aligning visual tokenizer pre-training with downstream generative objectives (reconstructing clean signals from heavily corrupted latents via noise interpolation and masking) is conceptually clean, well-motivated, and elegant.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across diverse generative paradigms: The paper evaluates six distinct generative models spanning non-autoregressive flow/diffusion (DiT, SiT, LightningDiT) and autoregressive models (MAR, RandomAR, RasterAR), rather than restricting evaluation to a single architecture family.

Significant empirical performance gains: The proposed tokenizer (l-DeTok) yields substantial improvements without modifying generative model architectures (e.g., boosting MAR-B FID from 2.31 to 1.55, matching original MAR-H, and pushing MAR-L to 1.35), all without relying on large-scale pretrained visual encoders (like DINOv2 or CLIP).

Valuable empirical insight for the community: The paper uncovers a key limitation of recent semantics-distilled continuous tokenizers (e.g., VA-VAE, MAETok)—namely, that while they benefit diffusion models, they fail drastically on autoregressive models (e.g., MAR FID degrades to 16.66).

Thorough ablations and reproducible details: The paper provides in-depth ablations on interpolative vs. additive noise, noise variance, masking ratio, constant vs. random masking, and joint training, alongside complete training cost and pseudo-code in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation domain limited to ImageNet 256x256: The experiments are solely conducted on class-conditional ImageNet generation at 256x256 resolution. Demonstrating scalability to higher resolutions (e.g., 512x512) or open-domain text-to-image datasets would significantly strengthen the claims.

Decoder train/test distribution gap requires multi-stage mitigation: The tokenizer decoder is trained on heavily corrupted latents, creating a distribution mismatch at inference where generative models supply relatively clean latents. Addressing this via an additional 100-epoch fine-tuning stage is effective but adds complexity to the training pipeline.

Scope limited to continuous tokenizers: The method is strictly applied to continuous latent spaces (like MAR and diffusion/flow transformers) and does not explore discrete vector-quantized (VQ) representations commonly used in classical autoregressive models.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and well-motivated core idea: viewing generative modeling through a unified denoising lens and aligning tokenizer training with downstream generative objectives via latent interpolative noising and masking.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across diverse generative paradigms, benchmarking six representative generative models spanning non-autoregressive (DiT, SiT, LightningDiT) and autoregressive (MAR, RandomAR, RasterAR) methods.
Broad applicability demonstrated across architectural backbones (ViT vs. CNN), latent topologies (2D vs. 1D tokenizers), and quantization schemes (continuous vs. discrete VQ).

Strong empirical improvements without relying on heavy external pretrained teacher models (such as DINOv2 or CLIP distillation), while demonstrating that semantic distillation can be combined orthogonally for further gains.

Thorough ablations and practical insights, including the comparison between interpolative vs. additive noise, noise schedules, masking distributions, and addressing the grokking phenomenon in 1D tokenizers.
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical analysis: while the empirical gains are consistent and strong, the paper provides limited theoretical explanation or latent space analysis (e.g., manifold smoothness, spectrum analysis) to explain why the representations become easier for downstream models to predict.

Inherent train-inference discrepancy in the tokenizer decoder: the decoder is trained primarily on heavily corrupted latents but evaluated on relatively clean latents during generative inference, requiring a secondary fine-tuning stage to bridge the gap.
Experiments are centered around ImageNet-1k and MS-COCO at moderate scales; evaluation on open-domain, web-scale datasets or modalities like video generation remains unexplored.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and effective core idea: training visual tokenizers with latent denoising (interpolative latent Gaussian noise and randomized patch masking) aligns the latent space with downstream generative denoising dynamics.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across diverse generative paradigms, including non-autoregressive (DiT, SiT, LightningDiT) and autoregressive (MAR, RandomAR, RasterAR) models, as well as 1D continuous and discrete VQ tokenizers.

Substantial and consistent empirical gains across benchmarks: on ImageNet 256x256, MAR-B improves from 2.31 to 1.55 FID (matching MAR-Huge), and MAR-L reaches 1.35 FID without requiring pretrained semantic teachers (e.g., DINOv2 or CLIP).

Insightful analysis of tokenizer transferability, demonstrating that prior semantics-distilled tokenizers (e.g., VA-VAE, MAETok) degrade when applied to autoregressive models, whereas l-DeTok generalizes robustly across both AR and non-AR architectures.

Extensive ablations covering noise mechanisms (interpolative vs. additive, noise variance, schedules), masking strategies, training dynamics (such as the grokking phase in 1D tokenizers), and decoder fine-tuning, accompanied by transparent reporting of computational overhead.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation remains largely intuitive; a deeper analytical characterization of the geometric or spectral properties of the latent manifold induced by latent denoising is left for future work.

There exists a training-test discrepancy on the decoder side (trained with corrupted latents, but tested on nearly clean generated latents), necessitating an extra decoder fine-tuning stage to achieve peak reconstruction and generative quality.

Evaluation on open-domain text-to-image synthesis is restricted to the relatively small-scale MS-COCO benchmark, with larger modern web-scale text-to-image setups and higher resolutions left unaddressed.

strengths: Compelling and conceptually intuitive core insight: viewing both diffusion (continuous noise corruption) and autoregressive modeling (masking corruption) under a unified denoising perspective, and directly aligning tokenizer training with this downstream objective.

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation across six diverse generative models spanning both autoregressive (MAR, RandomAR, RasterAR) and non-autoregressive (DiT, SiT, LightningDiT) paradigms.

Broad architectural applicability: the denoising principle is thoroughly evaluated not only on standard 2D continuous ViT tokenizers, but also across CNN-based autoencoders, 1D continuous tokenizers, and discrete vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizers.

Substantial and consistent empirical gains across benchmarks: achieves remarkable improvements on ImageNet 256x256 and 512x512 without requiring semantic distillation from heavy pretrained visual models (e.g., MAR-B FID improves from 2.31 to 1.55, matching original MAR-Huge; MAR-L achieves 1.35 FID).

High clarity and transparent reporting: rigorous ablations on noise schedules, interpolative vs. additive noise, masking ratios, and insightful discussion on the 1D tokenizer grokking dynamics and decoder fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical analysis: While the empirical results are convincing and reproducible, the underlying mathematical and geometric mechanism explaining why latent interpolative denoising reshapes the latent space to be more amenable to generative priors remains largely empirical.

Reconstruction vs. generation trade-off: As shown in Appendix B.1, injecting latent noise degrades reconstruction quality (rFID / rPSNR) while enhancing downstream generative metrics. A more explicit and systematic characterization of the Pareto frontier between reconstruction fidelity and generation quality would offer deeper practical guidance.
